units.sentence: The law doesn't require the rapid notification or guaranteed phone access Gazmararian described, and it sets no time limit for reaching parents.
units.marker: {analysis: checked the full enacted text (P-001 to P-019, P-056 to P-061); its communication rules are P-011 and P-059}
units.problem: Confirmed: no speed, notification-time or guaranteed-access requirement in the enacted text. The only device exception is P-013's plan-based one, plus P-007's general 'or required by law'.

units.sentence: How well school alert systems will reach families in a real crisis, since our sources have no data on how they perform.
Critics say enforcement will fall on teachers and administrators and lead to confrontations; in Florida, suspensions rose at first.
units.evidence_span: he worries the bill would put the burden on teachers and administrators to police phones, a task that can invite conflict
units.problem: The sources contain only one critic, teacher Darryl Adams. He 'worries' the bill 'would' burden staff with 'a task that can invite conflict'. 'Critics say ... will ... lead to confrontations' makes him plural and turns a possibility into a prediction. The Florida part is supported (P-039).
units.suggested_fix: 'A teacher worries enforcement would fall on teachers and administrators and can invite conflict; in Florida, suspensions rose at first.'

units.sentence: Teacher Darryl Adams said he worries the bill would put the burden on teachers and administrators to police phones, a task that can invite conflict.
units.evidence_span: said he worries the bill would put the burden on teachers and administrators to police phones, a task that can invite conflict

units.sentence: He said, 'We have a lot of older teachers that do not want to have that confrontation.'
units.evidence_span: We have a lot of older teachers that do not want to have that confrontation

units.sentence: Each school system must monitor and enforce the rules, which may include assigning staff and auditing phone storage.
units.evidence_span: which may include, but need not be limited to, assigning designated school personnel to oversee implementation

units.sentence: Consequences can include taking students' devices.
units.evidence_span: verbal warnings, confiscation of personal electronic devices, parental notification

units.sentence: In Florida, suspensions rose in the short term after phone bans, especially among Black students.
units.evidence_span: led to a significant increase in student suspensions in the short-term, especially among Black students

units.sentence: Supporters such as Sen. Sally Harrell say similar rules have worked in other high schools.
units.evidence_span: It has been done in high schools already
units.problem: Minor: Harrell's statement says nothing about enforcement burden or conflict, so it doesn't directly rebut this card's claim; see framing.

units.sentence: In Florida, the rise in suspensions began to fade after the first year.
units.evidence_span: disciplinary actions began to dissipate after the first year

units.sentence: Districts choose their own storage and enforcement methods.
units.evidence_span: The bill does not require a single statewide enforcement method, leaving districts to decide
units.problem: Minor: districts choose within required elements, such as progressive consequences (P-012) and monitoring (P-014).

units.sentence: No source we reviewed measured teacher or staff workload.
units.marker: {analysis: none of the archived sources includes workload data}

units.sentence: How much work each district's approach will create, since district policies were not part of our sources.
Critics say older students should keep some phone access, as a family choice and a way to learn responsible use.
units.evidence_span: high school students, who are older and often more independent, should be allowed to keep access to their phones

units.sentence: Teacher Darryl Adams said high school students, who are older and often more independent, should be allowed to keep access to their phones.
units.evidence_span: Adams also argues that high school students, who are older and often more independent, should be allowed to keep access to their phones.

units.sentence: A Senate amendment from the senator for the 38th District would have let districts allow phones between classes for grades 9 to 12, and it failed, 13 to 38.
units.evidence_span: Senator Kemp of the 38th offered the following amendment #1
units.problem: Minor: P-027 names the sponsor (Senator Kemp of the 38th) but the document leaves him unnamed; see framing.

units.sentence: Among parents who oppose a ban, 45.5% said it should be the parents' choice and 41.9% said students need to learn responsible use.
units.evidence_span: Should be parental choice 45.5 (4.2) No way to reach child during emergency 74.8 (3.5) Phones needed for health tools/apps 26.6 (3.6) Phones needed for schoolwork 19.8 (2.9) Students need to learn responsible use 41.9 (4.2)
units.problem: Minor: SE 4.2 means about +/-8 points, so these two reasons are statistically indistinguishable; not stated.

units.sentence: Another 26.6% said phones are needed for health tools or apps, but the law allows a device only when a student's IEP, Section 504 plan or medical plan explicitly requires it.
units.evidence_span: Phones needed for health tools/apps 26.6 (3.6)
units.problem: (1) 'Another' suggests a separate group, but P-035's reasons are multi-select (the five sum to 208.6%), so the 26.6% overlaps the 45.5% and 41.9%. (2) 'only when' overstates P-013: P-007 also exempts access 'required by law', and P-017 lets schools provide their own devices.
units.suggested_fix: '26.6% said phones are needed for health tools or apps (parents could pick several reasons); the law's specific exception covers devices a student's IEP, Section 504 plan or medical plan explicitly requires.'

units.sentence: A 17-year-old student who testified told lawmakers that phones have become addictive for teens and said, 'Social media is the cigarette of our generation.'
units.evidence_span: told lawmakers that phones have become addictive for teens

units.sentence: In Florida, the effects of phone bans were larger in middle and high schools.
units.evidence_span: The effects of cellphone bans are more pronounced in middle and high school settings
units.problem: Accurate, but it drops P-040's reason: 'where student smartphone ownership is more common'. Used against the maturity argument, the omission suggests an age-based reason the study doesn't give; see framing.
units.suggested_fix: Add 'where more students own smartphones'.

units.sentence: Our sources don't measure whether teens learn responsible phone use with or without a ban.
units.marker: {analysis: none of the archived sources addresses this}

units.sentence: This is mainly a disagreement about who should decide and what school is for.

framing_issues.text: Who pays: ... In Florida, suspensions rose in the short term after phone bans, especially among Black students.
framing_issues.issue: Uneven evidence in Option B. 'Who pays' cites study evidence (Florida suspensions) without the same P-039 sentence's caveat that discipline 'began to dissipate after the first year'. 'Who benefits' (line 78) gives only parent expectations and a senator's hope, and leaves out the Florida test-score gains (P-040). Costs get research; benefits get opinion.

framing_issues.text: What challenges it: The English study's summary lists well-being and phone use as its outcomes ... Its authors said their findings 'do not provide evidence to support' ...
framing_issues.issue: The English study is placed against the learning claim (card 1), which it never measured. On card 2 (mental health), its actual subject, the document says 'No one ... disputed this directly' (line 115). The counterevidence sits on the wrong claim and is missing from 'Who disagrees' on the right one.

framing_issues.text: Critics say enforcement will fall on teachers and administrators and lead to confrontations (card title line 144: 'will burden school staff and cause conflict')
framing_issues.issue: One named teacher becomes 'Critics', and his 'can invite conflict' becomes 'will ... cause conflict'. This overstates how widely and how firmly the concern is held, and makes it easier to rebut.

framing_issues.text: Hilton said districts reported 'improved focus and less isolation among younger students'
framing_issues.issue: A reporter's paraphrase is shown in quotation marks as the sponsor's own words, and a secondhand, unquantified claim is filed under 'What supports it'. The caveat on line 117 helps but doesn't fix the quote marks.

framing_issues.text: Another 26.6% said phones are needed for health tools or apps, but the law allows a device only when ...
framing_issues.issue: On the opponents' side, a survey reason gets an inline 'but the law...' rebuttal. Supporters' survey reasons (lines 78, 101, 113) get no such qualifier. 'Another' also implies non-overlapping groups in a multi-select question.

framing_issues.text: In Florida, the effects of phone bans were larger in middle and high schools.
framing_issues.issue: Missing context: the study links the larger effects to higher smartphone ownership, not to students' maturity. Placed against the 'old enough to manage their own phones' argument, the cut invites an inference the study doesn't make.

framing_issues.text: What supports it: Harrell said legislators want to hear teachers say, 'I can just teach again.' Woods told lawmakers he had heard nothing but support from teachers...
framing_issues.issue: Neither item is evidence that phone limits are working: one states what legislators hope to hear, the other reports teacher support for the bill. Harrell's 'done in high schools already' (line 125) also doesn't say Georgia, though the card title does. The 'Evidence: Uncertain' label softens this but doesn't cure it.

framing_issues.text: Who disagrees: Supporters such as Sen. Sally Harrell say similar rules have worked in other high schools.
framing_issues.issue: Harrell's general success claim doesn't address enforcement burden or staff conflict, so filing it as a rebuttal makes the counterargument look more on-point than it is.

framing_issues.text: An Emory public health professor, Julie Gazmararian, said parents' concerns about emergency access are 'valid and understandable.'
framing_issues.issue: One two-sentence quote is split. The first half is filed as support for the concern and the 'However, effective cellphone policies can address this' half as a challenge. Her overall position, that the concern can be addressed, is not visible in either place alone.

framing_issues.text: Adams said that when two of his daughters were in a lockdown, he could not get updates for hours.
framing_issues.issue: Presented as support that bans cut family contact, but P-049 doesn't say the daughters' phones were restricted or why updates were unavailable.

framing_issues.text: Who benefits: Students and families could reach each other between classes.
framing_issues.issue: Uneven caveats in Option C. The benefit is stated without the 'in districts that chose' condition, which the matching cost on line 87 includes.

framing_issues.text: The margin of error is about 4 points either way.
framing_issues.issue: Only the overall margin is given. Subgroup percentages used throughout (opponents' reasons, SE 2.9-4.2, about +/-6 to 8 points; supporters' reasons, SE 1.8-2.9) are much less precise, and opponents are only about 29% of 1,002 respondents.

framing_issues.text: The rules that already covered younger students in public schools now apply through 12th grade. (also line 8 'can't use')
framing_issues.issue: Present tense ('now apply', 'can't use') suggests the high school ban is already in force. The Act takes effect Dec 31, 2026 and the high school ban starts by July 1, 2027.

framing_issues.text: By Jan 1 each year: Every district must adopt or update its device policy, now covering kindergarten through 12th grade.
framing_issues.issue: Missing context: with the Act effective Dec 31, 2026, the first 'By January 1 each year' deadline (P-008) is arguably Jan 1, 2027, six months before the latest high school start (July 1, 2027, P-007). The document lists both dates without saying how they interact, so readers may be unsure when K-12 policies are due. This is an interpretive question to flag, not settle.

framing_issues.text: Still true / Also new in this law (lines 52-62)
framing_issues.issue: The headings claim continuity or novelty that the passages don't show for (a)(5), (g), (h) and the dual-enrollment wording in (c)(3). No prior-law text for those provisions is in the passages.

framing_issues.text: A Senate amendment from the senator for the 38th District ...
framing_issues.issue: The amendment's sponsor is left unnamed while every other legislator is named; P-027 names 'Senator Kemp of the 38th'. Naming him, with a note that he is not Gov. Brian Kemp, would be consistent.

framing_issues.text: Woods told lawmakers ... according to Atlanta News First.
framing_issues.issue: Uneven attribution hedge: only Woods's reported statement gets 'according to' the outlet. Harrell's and Adams's reported statements from the same outlet don't. The outlet name also doesn't appear in the passages.

framing_issues.text: Who pays: State School Superintendent Richard Woods said extending the ban would 'end the harm caused by constant technology access and interruption.'
framing_issues.issue: The cost of the status quo rests on an advocate's characterization ('the harm') rather than evidence. It is attributed, but it is the only 'Who pays' item that isn't an inference.
